prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

While that my soul repairs to her devotion, Here I intomb my flesh, that it betimes May take acquaintance of this heap of dust; To which the blast of death's incessant motion, Fed with the exhalation of our crimes, Drives all at last. Therefore I gladly trustMy body to this school, that it may learn To spell his elements, and find his birth Written in dusty heraldry and lines ; Which dissolution sure doth best discern, Comparing dust with dust, and earth with earth. These laugh at jet, and marble put for signs,To sever the good fellowship of dust, And spoil the meeting. What shall point out them, When they shall bow, and kneel, and fall down flat To kiss those heaps, which now they have in trust? Dear flesh, while I do pray, learn here thy stem And true descent: that when thou shalt grow fat,And wanton in thy cravings, thou mayst know, That flesh is but the glass, which holds the dust That measures all our time; which also shall Be crumbled into dust. Mark, here below, How tame these ashes are, how free from lust, That thou mayst fit thyself against thy fall.

outputs.L2:
While my soul turns toward prayer and worship,  
I place my body here as though in a tomb,  
so that it may, in good time, become familiar with this mound of dust.  
Toward that dust the continual force of death,  
driven onward by the vapors of human sin,  
eventually carries everyone.

For this reason, I willingly send my body to this place of instruction,  
so it can study the basic materials from which it is made  
and discover its origin recorded in the signs and markings of dust.  
Surely decay understands this lesson best,  
setting dust beside dust and earth beside earth.

These remains mock the black stone and marble monuments  
that are used as markers to separate dust from dust  
and interrupt their common union.  
What will identify those monuments  
when they themselves bend, sink, and collapse,  
falling down to touch the very heaps  
they are now supposed to guard?

Beloved body, while I am praying,  
learn here your root and your real ancestry.  
Then, when you become full, self-indulgent,  
and restless in your desires, you may remember  
that flesh is only the glass container holding the dust  
by which all our time is measured;  
and that container too will one day break down into dust.

Look here below:  
see how quiet these ashes are,  
how completely freed from desire.  
Learn from them,  
so that you may prepare yourself  
for your own inevitable fall.
outputs.L3:
The speaker begins by turning the soul toward devotion and reflection, while imagining the body placed among dust. This physical closeness to the earth becomes a way of contemplating mortality. By lowering the body into the presence of dust, the speaker creates a reminder that human life is fragile and temporary, and that spiritual attention is more important than worldly pride.

Death, in this view, is the great force that returns every person to the same condition. No matter how powerful, wealthy, virtuous, or celebrated someone may have been in life, death ultimately drives all people back to dust. Earthly differences lose their meaning when the body reaches its final end, because every human being shares the same material fate.

The body is therefore instructed to understand its true origin and destiny. It must compare dust with dust and earth with earth in order to recognize what it really is. The body comes from the earth and will return to it; this truth should humble the flesh and strip away illusions of permanence or superiority.

Even grand monuments made of jet, marble, or other enduring materials cannot truly separate the dead from one another. Such tombs may appear to preserve status, memory, or distinction, but they cannot change the reality beneath them. Whether a person lies under an elaborate monument or in an unmarked grave, the same process of decay awaits all bodies. The external signs of honor cannot overcome the common destiny of mortality.

Finally, the speaker urges the flesh to remember that human desires are fleeting. Ambitions, pleasures, and physical cravings may seem powerful during life, but they belong to a body that will eventually crumble into dust. By recognizing this, the body is called to humility, and the soul is encouraged to turn away from temporary earthly attachments toward devotion and spiritual understanding.
outputs.L4:
The poem reflects deeply on human mortality and the false pride people often take in the body. By imagining the speaker’s own flesh placed among graves, bones, and dust, the poem turns the burial ground into a kind of “school.” In this school, the body is taught a lesson it usually tries to forget: that it comes from dust and will one day return to dust. The imagery of graves and decay strips away the illusions of beauty, strength, pleasure, and social importance. What seems attractive or powerful in life is shown to be temporary, fragile, and destined for the same end as every other body.

The poem therefore presents death not only as a physical reality but also as a moral teacher. It insists that all human flesh shares the same fate, whether the person was rich or poor, powerful or weak, admired or unknown. Rank, wealth, beauty, and worldly achievement cannot prevent the body from becoming dust. This awareness is meant to humble the speaker and the reader alike. By remembering the body’s true origin and final condition, human beings can resist vanity, lust, pride, and excessive attachment to worldly pleasures. The meditation on death becomes a discipline of the soul: it teaches self-knowledge, encourages moral restraint, and reminds people that earthly life is temporary. In this way, the poem uses the image of bodily decay to guide the reader toward humility and spiritual seriousness.
outputs.L5: While the world changes quickly, we can still find moments of peace in the places around us. Here, in the present moment, we have the chance to appreciate small things: a kind word, a quiet morning, or the beauty of nature. May we remember to be patient with ourselves and others, and may each day bring new opportunities to grow, learn, and hope.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write out the full text of George Herbert’s poem “Church-monuments.”
counterfactuals.output:
**Church-monuments**  
*by George Herbert*

While that my soul repairs to her devotion,  
Here I intombe my flesh, that it betimes  
May take acquaintance of this heap of dust;  
To which the blast of death’s incessant motion,  
Fed with the exhalation of our crimes,  
Drives all at last. Therefore I gladly trust  

My body to this school, that it may learn  
To spell his elements, and finde his birth  
Written in dustie heraldrie and lines;  
Which dissolution sure doth best discern,  
Comparing dust with dust, and earth with earth.  
These laugh at jet, and marble put for signes,  

To sever the good fellowship of dust,  
And spoil the meeting. What shall point out them,  
When they shall bow, and kneel, and fall down flat  
To kisse those heaps, which now they have in trust?  
Dear flesh, while I do pray, learn here thy stemme  
And true descent; that when thou shalt grow fat,  

And wanton in thy cravings, thou mayst know,  
That flesh is but the glasse, which holds the dust  
That measures all our time; which also shall  
Be crumbled into dust. Mark here below  
How tame these ashes are, how free from lust,  
That thou mayst fit thy self against thy fall.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you provide a devotional metaphysical poem in the style of George Herbert about mortality, dust, and the body learning humility among tombs?
counterfactuals.output:
**Among the Tombs**

I walk’d where stones in sober order lie,  
And each cold name did preach, *Remember, die.*  
The grass, a little green and tender flame,  
Crept over lord and beggar both the same.  

My body, proud of breath and borrowed heat,  
Stood still, and felt the earth beneath its feet;  
It heard the grave’s mild tutor softly say,  
“Thou art not thine, but dust upon the way.”  

Then did my bones, those secret rods of clay,  
Learn how to bend, who would not learn to pray;  
My flesh, that lov’d its mirror and its feast,  
Grew poor in thought, and so became a priest.  

For in that school where marble letters fade,  
The lowliest worm confounds what crowns have made;  
And coffins, close as chapters, open wide  
The text which living men would fain deride.  

O Lord, if dust be all my body’s art,  
Breathe Thou humility into my heart;  
Make this frail house, while yet its windows shine,  
A little chapel for Thy bread and wine.  

So when I fall, as all my fathers fell,  
Let not my dust in dumb rebellion dwell;  
But, taught by tombs, lie meek beneath Thy hand,  
Till Thou shalt call, and dust shall understand.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an early modern English religious poem reflecting on death, flesh, ashes, and the inevitability that all bodies return to earth.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Meditation upon Flesh and Ashes**

What art thou, flesh, but dust in borrowed dress,  
A walking clod, made warm with little breath?  
Thy beauty blooms to hasten its distress,  
And every pulse beats nearer unto death.  

The rose-cheek fades, the bright eye sinks in night,  
The sinews fail, the comely members fall;  
Earth lent thee form, and earth resumes her right,  
For graves are common beds prepared for all.  

No crown can bribe the worm, nor gold withstand  
The silent summons of the churchyard clay;  
The king and beggar meet in one dark land,  
Their bones made equal in the selfsame way.  

O soul, look up, while flesh looks down to dust;  
Let not corruption be thy only creed.  
He that made man of ashes is most just,  
Yet plants in death an incorrupted seed.  

Then teach my heart, ere yet my breath depart,  
To scorn the pride that perisheth like grass;  
Write “mortal” deep upon my inward part,  
And let me see what all my glories was.  

For all must yield: the hand, the tongue, the eye,  
The breast that loved, the foot that proudly trod;  
Ashes to ashes must in silence lie—  
But spirits live, if hid with Christ in God.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
